Corporate Bitcoin Treasuries

The Index Was the Buyer

MSCI drops Strategy from its global equity benchmarks at the close of November, forcing $1.6 billion in passive index-fund sales and puncturing the premium that financed the corporate treasury machine.

Analysis by Roger and dispatch from Bitcoin Magazine

On the final trading day of November, a slice of the largest corporate bitcoin treasury will be auctioned off to whoever wants it, and nobody involved in the transaction will have expressed a view on the asset. MSCI’s November index review, released shortly after five o’clock New York time on Wednesday, confirmed the deletion of Strategy from the MSCI USA Index at the close of November 30, taking it simultaneously out of MSCI World and ACWI [s566]. As Roger observed in an exhaustive accounting of the balance sheet, On the first morning of December, a slice of Strategy's shareholder base will be gone, and nobody will have made a decision about bitcoin. [s569]

The exclusion was enacted under a broad non-operating issuer rule requiring a company’s operating assets to equal at least half of its total assets. Nowhere in the rule that did it does the word bitcoin appear. [s569] The same neutral screen also removed Japan’s Metaplanet, the United Kingdom’s Yellow Cake uranium vehicle, Iceland’s Skel Fjárfestingafélag, and micro-cap Upexi [s566]. While Strategy’s forced selling involves roughly 13 million shares—about 3.1 percent of basic shares outstanding, valued near $1.6 billion—that volume is less than a single typical trading day [s569]. The real structural consequence is not the size of the turnover; it is the evaporation of the passive equity bid that drove the treasury acquisition flywheel.

Strategy’s accumulation model was an arbitrage built on the gap between equity market capitalization and the value of its underlying 850,364 coins. When equity traded above net asset value, issuing shares accreted bitcoin per share for every existing holder. With the common equity now trading around 0.83 times the spot value of its coins—with roughly sixteen billion dollars of senior convertible debt and preferred shares standing ahead of common stockholders—the mechanism has reversed [s569]. Recent weekly disclosures reveal that out of $283.8 million raised through share sales, $188.3 million was deployed to retire its own 12 percent STRC preferred stock at $97.74 on the dollar, while just $81.9 million bought 1,036 bitcoin [s569]. As Roger noted, It is buying its own paper instead of the asset. That is what a fund does when its units trade below net asset value. It is not what a growth company does. [s569]

The physical layer beneath these financial vehicles experienced its own quiet compression. Daily block issuance revenue has dropped from $56.1 million when bitcoin was near $124,700 to $33.1 million at current spot levels near $73,433 [s569]. Yet at the base protocol, node software operated without incident. The coins do not care. That was always the point of them. [s569]

Institutional Rails

Deutsche Bank Switches on Custody for Institutions

Germany’s largest bank holds private keys in hardware modules as retail outages strike legacy payments.

Deutsche Bank went live on Wednesday with digital asset custody for paying corporate and institutional clients across Europe under European Union MiCA compliance [s565]. The bank manages keys in hardware security modules, offering cold and warm storage through its Autobahn portal, and signed an agreement with Deutsche Asset Management to explore tokenized funds [s565].

The announcement drew immediate reaction from sovereign infrastructure advocates. Coincards reminded holders that Bitcoin was built so you never have to hand your keys to a bank. [s109] The contrast was sharpened in Australia, where Westpac’s online banking and PayID networks went down for hours on Tuesday, stalling domestic transfers while Bitcoin blocks cleared uninterrupted [s70]. Simultaneously, Citigroup disclosed an expanded $119 million position in Fidelity’s FBTC and grew its BlackRock IBIT holdings by 50 percent during the third quarter [s560].

The Machine Mind

Rage Against the Slop: Craftsmanship in the Age of Tokens

hodlbod reflects on the loss of software idiosyncrasy to the machine, as builders grapple with commercial pressures.

Some people faint at the sight of blood. I am becoming increasingly nauseous at the sight of slop. [s533] Writing in an extended meditation on code and conviviality, hodlbod surveyed the post-industrial sludge of language model outputs sweeping modern developer workflows. The Machine is bleeding, or maybe we are. The sum of human knowledge and culture has been scraped, ingested, and sprayed across the internet. [s533]

Drawing on Ivan Illich’s critique of radical monopoly, hodlbod warned of tools that cease to be convivial when their scale forces compulsory adoption and atrophies natural human competence [s533]. The tension between autonomy and market compromise was echoed across the network. Highlighting hodlbod’s reflections on community software, Nate noted: Every effort I’ve made to bend Nostr to my potential customers’ will has resulted in compromise on the vision that got me into the space. [s531]

Protocol & Security

Stateful Contracts in Taproot Keys, and a Bug Held 396 Days

Salvatore Ingala drafts BIP 443, while Bitcoin Core discloses an embargoed reorg template vulnerability.

Developer Salvatore Ingala authored BIP 443 proposing OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY (OP_CCV), which commits contract state directly into Taproot output keys via key tweaking [s559]. The proposal enables stateful UTXOs that update committed data across consecutive transactions on-chain, unlocking compact fraud proofs without relying on a trusted off-chain sequencer [s559].

Meanwhile, Bitcoin Core published three patched security advisories, disclosing CVE-2025-62861 after an intentional 396-day embargo [s569]. The high-severity bug in version-3 transaction eviction logic could leave a node gossiping normally during a chain reorganization while unable to assemble block templates until restarted [s569]. The fix shipped in versions 28.3, 29.2, and 30.0 in October 2025, held until older releases went end-of-life, with zero funds ever at risk [s569]. Across the ecosystem, Freedom Tech logged a 36-release day led by LNbits 1.7.1 and Stack Wallet 2.7.5 [s555].
